variants.name: Boost.Asio composed async_write (callback chain)
variants.implementation_notes: The modern C++ default is Boost.Asio's composed operation: one async_write sleeps until the previous buffer has been fully handed to the socket, so a producer that starts the next write from inside the completion handler is paced by the peer and by the kernel send buffer - the callback chain replaces the classic queue-and-block structure entirely. Because the protocol is a free function, only one async_write may be outstanding per socket or the buffers interleave; keep the messages in a std::deque and pop the front in the handler. Asio does not bound what you queue yourself, so the outbound deque still needs an explicit capacity and a full policy (wait for the handler, drop, or close the session).
pitfalls: Two overlapping async_write calls on one socket interleave and corrupt the stream; serialize with a single outbound deque.
The buffer passed to async_write must stay alive and unmoved until the completion handler runs - moving or reallocating the deque element is a classic dangling-buffer bug.
A single-threaded io_context must never run blocking work inside the completion handler: it stops accepting and writing for every other connection.
Asio's per-operation buffering is unbounded from the application's point of view; the bound has to be your deque.

variants.name: Bounded queue with std::counting_semaphore / condition_variable
variants.implementation_notes: Outside Asio, the portable C++ structure is a bounded deque plus std::condition_variable (producer waits while full, consumer signals not_full), and since C++20 std::counting_semaphore gives the permit form directly: acquire() before enqueue blocks when the bound is reached, release() after the consumer takes an item. Use the semaphore when a permit is enough (the queue itself can stay lock-protected or single-producer/single-consumer) and the condition variable when you also need a predicate (shutdown, flush, priority). Both are the same hand-written structure the classic pattern describes - the standard library only supplies the primitives, never the queue.
pitfalls: counting_semaphore::try_acquire can fail spuriously, so a reliable non-blocking check needs a retry loop and a bounded wait needs try_acquire_for/try_acquire_until.
Forgetting release() on an exception path shrinks the bound permanently until the stage stops accepting work.
Destructing a counting_semaphore while a producer is blocked in acquire() is undefined/never safe; shut the pipeline down through a documented path.
Relying on condition_variable without a predicate (if instead of while, or without the mutex held) loses the bound under spurious wakeups.
